title: Van Helsing
full_review:
A legendary monster-hunter sets up stakes in Transylvania in the disjointed, distended and all-around dreadful action adventure "Van Helsing" (Universal).

One would think that a film containing Dracula, a werewolf and Frankenstein's monster would be a can't-miss. Think again. Full of headache-inducing action sequences, the clumsily structured film is more lumbering than Frankenstein's monster, mostly due to a script that lacks any bite and that has enough stale dialogue to make an audience howl with laughter -- full moon or not.

Hugh Jackman stars as Gabriel Van Helsing, a notorious bounty hunter working for a clandestine Vatican agency charged with ridding the world of fiendish creatures; of course, a much greater service would be ridding the world of awful films. Conflicted over his violent vocation, Van Helsing justifies his enigmatic employment partly as a penance for past crimes, the details of which remain shrouded even to him thanks to an inexplicable amnesia. "Some things are better left forgotten," he concludes -- starting with this movie.

After a roughhouse round of Hyde-and-seek with a digitally created Mr. Hyde (voiced by Robbie Coltrane) in the bell tower of Paris' Notre Dame Cathedral (one can only assume Quasimodo is subletting), the holy hired gun is summoned back to Rome. There he is given new marching orders: Travel to Transylvania and terminate Dracula (Richard Roxburgh) before the count kills the sole surviving scion of a royal bloodline of vampire hunters, Princess Valerious (Kate Beckinsale), who is bent on avenging her ancestors and ending an ancient curse on her family.

Accompanied by a mousy monk, Friar Carl (David Wenham), Van Helsing heads off to Transylvania where he teams up with Valerious. Of course, with all the wooden stakes and crucifixes they had to pack, little room was left in their saddlebags for a plot. The rest of the supernatural silliness involves little more than Van Helsing going against Dracula and his blood-sucking brides (Elena Anaya, Silvia Colloca and Josie Maran), who transform into bat-like demons and terrorize the local village with aerial assaults. Along the way he also tussles with werewolves, finds an unlikely ally in Frankenstein's monster (played with humanity by Shuler Hensley) and foils a diabolical plot by Dracula, serving as a reminder that even counts should never count their eggs before they're hatched. Emotionally, nothing is at, er, stake.

As directed by Stephen Sommers (who also helmed the equally overwrought "The Mummy" and "The Mummy's Return"), the long, loud and ludicrous affair unfolds as a series of dizzying, albeit visually spectacular, special-effects sequences, wrapped in appropriately dark and rainy gothic atmospherics without the slightest concern for narrative coherence -- or, for that matter, spatial relations. For a far more fun take on the Transylvanian trio, rent 1948's "Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein."

Jackman is appealing as the grim slayer. Roxburgh tries to inject some life into the undead Dracula, but the material doesn't give him much to sink his teeth into.

In a nod to political correctness, Sommers has made the clandestine Vatican bureau Van Helsing works for a syncretistic stew of interfaith employees -- including Buddhist monks and Muslim imams -- a choice that may irk some Catholics, as may a scene involving Friar Carl requesting sexual favors as reward for saving a village maiden.

One highlight involves a lavish masquerade ball shot in the de-consecrated church of St. Nicholas in Prague and choreographed by Debra Brown of the famed Cirque du Soleil.

In its heyday, Universal produced some of the most iconic horror films in Hollywood history, including the landmark "Dracula" (1931) staring Bela Lugosi, Boris Karloff's "Frankenstein" (1931) and "The Wolf Man" (1941) staring Lon Chaney Jr. The film opens with a stylish black-and-white tribute to those films in which a mob of angry villagers brandishing pitchforks and torches storm Frankenstein's castle. Universal is lucky that irate moviegoers don't do the same at cinemas.

Toward the end of the movie, Frankenstein's monster bemoans the fact that he is "accustomed to pain," but by that point so is the audience.

Due to incessant comic-book violence, an implied sexual encounter, some innuendo and frightening images, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
